title: John at the Table
subtitle: Seven sessions walking a seeker straight through the Gospel of John, one sign at a time
summary: John wrote his Gospel with one purpose he states out loud, that you may believe and have life. This study takes a seeker straight through John in seven sessions, one sign at a time, from the Word made flesh to the empty tomb. It does not argue and it does not push. It reads the text out loud, asks what it says, and lets Jesus be the one who is compelling. A person who does not yet believe can sit at this table and never be cornered, because the study only asks two things, that you read honestly and that you say what you actually think.
setting: A table with a Gospel of John open. Bring your real questions. No one has to pretend to believe anything to be here.
forWho: A person who does not yet believe but is willing to read one Gospel with honest company, and the friend reading it alongside them.
rhythm: Seven sessions, one passage of John each time, no pressure to decide anything, only to read and to talk honestly.
leaderNote: John wrote his Gospel with a single stated purpose, that the reader may believe and have life, so let John do the work. Do not argue. Read the text, ask what it says, and let Jesus be the one who is compelling. The seeker should feel invited, never cornered.

sessions.title: The Word Became Flesh
sessions.bigIdea: John does not start with a manger or a miracle. He starts before time, and he tells you the Word who made everything walked into the world he made and took on skin.
sessions.open: When you hear that God became a man, what is your first honest reaction, and where did that reaction come from?
sessions.read: Read John 1:1-5 out loud, and then verse 14. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
observe: Count how many things John says the Word did before verse 5. What is being claimed about who made the world?
Verse 14 says the Word became flesh. What is startling about a writer putting God and flesh in the same sentence?
talk: John could have opened with a birth story. He reaches back before the beginning instead. If the claim is that the maker of everything moved into the neighborhood, what would that change about how you read the rest of this book?
The light shines in the darkness and the darkness has not overcome it. Where in your own life does that sentence sound like hope, and where does it sound too good to be true? Say the honest one.
Dwelt among us is a plain word for moved in and stayed. Not a visit. Why might it matter that God came close instead of shouting from a distance?
sessions.practice: Read John chapter 1 on your own this week, slowly, one time. Mark one line that drew you in and one line that made you stop. Bring both back to the table.
sessions.send: You do not have to believe it tonight. You have to hear what John is claiming. The maker of everything came near enough to touch.
sessions.passItOn: Think of one person who would read a Gospel if someone read it with them. Ask them to come next time. A table with one more honest reader is a better table.

sessions.title: Come and See
sessions.bigIdea: The first followers of Jesus were not argued into anything. They were invited to come and look, and the invitation is the same one on this table tonight.
sessions.open: Think of a time you were talked into something and a time you were simply shown something. Which one actually changed your mind, and why?
sessions.read: Read John 1:35-46. John the Baptist sees Jesus walk by and says, behold, the Lamb of God. Two of his followers start following Jesus, and Jesus turns and asks them, what are you seeking. They ask where he is staying, and he answers, come and you will see. One of them, Andrew, goes and finds his brother Simon and brings him to Jesus. The next day Jesus finds Philip, and Philip finds Nathanael, who is skeptical and asks whether anything good can come out of Nazareth. Philip does not argue with him. Philip says, come and see.
observe: The very first thing Jesus says in this Gospel is a question. What is the question, and why might a question be a strange way to start gathering followers?
Nathanael starts out doubtful. What exactly does Philip say back to the doubt?
talk: Come and see is not a sales pitch. It asks for a look, not a signature. What is the difference between being sold something and being invited to see for yourself, and which one is happening at this table?
Jesus asks what are you seeking before he offers anyone anything. If he asked you that tonight, what is the honest answer, even if the answer is that you are not sure you are seeking anything?
Nathanael doubted out loud and was not shamed for it. He was invited to look. What would it mean for this table to be a place where the doubt gets said out loud and stays welcome?
sessions.practice: This week, ask yourself the question Jesus asked, what are you seeking, and write down the first true answer, not the polished one. Bring it if you are willing.
sessions.send: Nobody here has to be argued into anything. The whole invitation is two words. Come and see.
sessions.passItOn: Andrew heard about Jesus and immediately went and got his brother. Who is the one person you would go get? Ask them to the next session the way Andrew did his.

sessions.title: He Knows What You Actually Thirst For
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus keeps meeting people at the level of their deepest thirst. He turns water into wine at a wedding and offers a stranger at a well a water that ends thirst for good.
sessions.open: What is something you chased hard, got, and found it did not satisfy the way you expected? No judgment at this table.
sessions.read: First, a quick picture from earlier in John. At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out, and Jesus quietly turns six stone jars of water into the best wine of the night, in John 2:1-11, the first of his signs. Then read John 4:7-14. Jesus, tired from the road, sits at a well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, which already breaks the rules of who was allowed to talk to whom. She is surprised. Jesus tells her that if she knew who was asking, she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water. He says, everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.
observe: Jesus starts by asking her for something. How does the conversation flip from him needing a drink to him offering one?
He says ordinary water leaves you thirsty again. What is he saying about the difference between what she came to the well for and what he is offering?
talk: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again. Name the wells people keep going back to, the ones that never quite fill you. Which well is yours right now?
Jesus crossed a hard line just to talk to this woman, a line of gender and race and reputation. What does it tell you that he went out of his way for the person everyone else avoided?
Living water that ends thirst is a big claim. You do not have to buy it tonight. But if it were true, what in you is thirsty enough to want it to be?
sessions.practice: Notice one time this week when you reach for a well that never fully satisfies, a screen, a purchase, a drink, the phone, approval. Do not scold yourself. Just write down what you were actually thirsty for underneath it.
sessions.send: He asked a tired stranger for water and offered her a spring that never runs dry. He tends to know the thirst under the thirst.
sessions.passItOn: This woman ran back to her town and told everyone about the man at the well. Who in your world is thirsty and honest? Invite them to come sit at this well next time.

sessions.title: The Bread of Life
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus makes a claim so large that a crowd walks away from it. He does not chase them or soften it. He turns to the few who stay and lets them decide.
sessions.open: When have you watched a lot of people quit something all at once? What made the ones who stayed decide to stay?
sessions.read: Read John 6:35. Jesus said, I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst. This comes right after he has fed thousands with a few loaves, and the crowd wants more bread. Jesus offers them himself instead, and it is a harder word than they came for. Then read John 6:66-69. After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, do you want to go away as well. Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go. You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.
observe: The crowd wanted more bread and Jesus offered them himself. Why might that be a harder thing to accept than another free meal?
When the crowd leaves, Jesus does not water down the claim to keep them. What does that tell you about whether he is trying to sell anything?
talk: I am the bread of life is not a modest thing to say. It is either too much or exactly enough. Whichever it is to you tonight, say which, and why.
Jesus lets people walk away. He gives them a real door out. How does it change the invitation to know that leaving is genuinely allowed here too?

Peter does not say he has it all figured out. He says, to whom shall we go, you have the words of eternal life. Have you ever stayed with something not because you were certain but because everything else felt emptier? What was that like?
sessions.practice: This week, sit with the question Peter asked as your own, to whom shall we go. Write down where else you have looked for the thing you are hungry for, and whether it fed you.
sessions.send: The crowd wanted bread for a day. He offered bread for good, and let them choose. The door out is open, which is what makes staying mean something.
sessions.passItOn: Peter answered for the whole table when he spoke up. Bring one person next time who has walked away from faith before. This is a study that lets people leave, which makes it safe to come back and look again.

sessions.title: I Once Was Blind
sessions.bigIdea: A man born blind is healed and then dragged through interrogations by people who can see fine but refuse to. The real blindness in the story is not in his eyes.
sessions.open: When have you kept an opinion long after the evidence turned against it, just because changing your mind was costly? Be honest.
sessions.read: Read John 9:1-7. Jesus and his followers pass a man who has been blind since birth, and they ask whose fault it is, his or his parents. Jesus refuses the blame question and says the works of God will be shown in him. Then Jesus spits on the ground, makes mud, spreads the mud on his eyes, and tells him to go wash in the pool of Siloam. The man goes, washes, and comes back seeing. What follows is a long fight, because the religious leaders do not want it to be true, and they question the man again and again. Read John 9:25, his plain answer to all of it. One thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see.
observe: The disciples want to assign blame for the blindness. How does Jesus change the question they are asking?
The leaders keep pressing the healed man for a theology he does not have. What is the one thing he refuses to stop saying?
talk: One thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. The man cannot win the debate, but he will not deny what happened to him. What is the difference between being able to argue for something and knowing it happened to you?
The people with working eyes are the ones who will not see. Where is it easiest for you to refuse to see something because seeing it would cost you? Nobody is grading you here.
Jesus threw out the blame question, whose fault is this. A lot of people carry the belief that their suffering is punishment. What would it do to set that question down the way Jesus did?
sessions.practice: This week, name one thing you know from your own life that you could not prove to a skeptic in an argument. Just notice that knowing and proving are not the same thing.
sessions.send: He could not out-argue the experts. He just would not deny his own eyes. That is a kind of honesty an argument cannot touch.
sessions.passItOn: This man told the truth about what he saw to everyone who would listen, and to plenty who would not. Bring one person next time who trusts what they have seen more than what they have been told. This story is for them.

sessions.title: The Resurrection and the Life
sessions.bigIdea: At the grave of his friend, Jesus does two things at once. He weeps like a man who has lost someone, and he raises the dead like the God who has not.
sessions.open: Tell the table about a grief that is still with you, only as much as you want to share. What did you most need from the people around you in it?
sessions.read: Jesus comes to Bethany four days after his friend Lazarus has died. Martha, the sister of Lazarus, meets him, and Jesus says to her, in John 11:25-26, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Then read John 11:33-44. When Jesus sees Mary weeping and the others weeping, he is deeply moved, and Jesus wept. He goes to the tomb, a cave with a stone across it, and asks them to take the stone away. He prays, and then he calls out with a loud voice, Lazarus, come out. And the man who had been dead four days walks out still wrapped in his grave cloths, and Jesus tells them to unbind him and let him go.
observe: Jesus knows he is about to raise Lazarus, and he weeps anyway. What does it say about him that he grieves at a grave he is about to open?
He calls Lazarus out by name. Why might it matter that the same voice that made the world in chapter 1 now calls one dead man out of a tomb?
talk: I am the resurrection and the life is a sentence spoken at a graveside, not in a classroom. If it is true, what does it change about the worst loss you have faced or fear facing? If you are not sure it is true, say what you would need it to be.
Jesus wept even though he had power over the death in front of him. What is the difference between a God who stays distant from your grief and one who cries at the grave with you?

Lazarus came out still bound in grave cloths and had to be unwrapped by the people around him. Where in your life are you alive but still bound, still wrapped in something old? You do not have to answer out loud.
sessions.practice: This week, if you carry a grief, do not rush past it. Sit with it for ten honest minutes, and if you pray, tell God the truth about it. Notice that in this story God does not scold the tears.
sessions.send: He wept at the grave and then he emptied it. Power that also weeps is a stranger thing than most people expect from God.
sessions.passItOn: Someone you know is standing at a grave right now, a real one or the kind that has no funeral. You do not need all the answers to sit with them. Bring them next time, or just go sit. This table will keep a seat.

sessions.title: That You May Believe
sessions.bigIdea: John finally tells you why he wrote the whole thing. Every sign, every conversation, every I am, was building to a cross, an empty tomb, and a decision he leaves in your hands.
sessions.open: Looking back over these seven weeks, what is one moment in John that has stayed with you, and why that one?
sessions.read: At the cross, after hours of it, Jesus says three words and then dies. Read John 19:30. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, it is finished, and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit. Finished, not defeated. A thing completed. Three days later the tomb is empty, and over the next chapter Jesus meets Mary in the garden, the disciples in a locked room, and Thomas, who said he would not believe without seeing the wounds, until he saw them. Then John steps out from behind the story and tells you his whole purpose. Read John 20:30-31. Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book, but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
observe: Jesus says it is finished, not I am finished. What is the difference between those two sentences at a cross?
In 20:30-31 John finally states his reason for the whole book. What are the two things he says he wants for the reader, and in what order?
talk: John admits he left things out and chose these signs on purpose, so that you may believe. Knowing he wrote to persuade, do you feel handled or do you feel leveled with? Say which, honestly.
Thomas doubted and was not thrown out. He was shown the wounds. What does it tell you that the book keeps making room for the doubter right up to the end?

The aim of John is not just that you believe something but that you have life. After seven weeks, where do you honestly stand tonight, and what is the one question you still carry? An I am not there is a real and welcome answer.
sessions.practice: Write down where you actually are after seven sessions, believing, doubting, somewhere in between, and the one question still open in you. Share it with one person from this table this week over coffee.
sessions.send: John told you plainly why he wrote it, so that you may believe and have life. You have read the whole thing now. The decision was always going to be yours, and it still is.
sessions.passItOn: This study happened because someone was willing to read a Gospel with you. You could do the same for a table of your own, exactly the way it was done for you. Name the two or three people you would read John with, and pick a week to begin.
